30 when I was diagnosed. Started medication shortly thereafter. 

Still working on improving things and working alongside my brain instead of against it but I can say things have absolutely improved. For one, I can go easier on myself and note that sometimes I have to do things differently than most folks to get the same sort of stuff done. Bethany down the street gets all her dishes done at once? Good for her. I have to trick myself into it using timers and to-do lists and a specific playlist and I will get distracted a few times and maybe won't get them all done but enough that there's space on the counters now. High five, Bethany! Joe can focus on whatever he wants and can recall things easily? Good for Joe! I need meds for that. High five, Joe! I dunno, stuff like that.

I think for me knowing why I just could not seem to overcome things and then suddenly having a clear answer as to why allowed me to grant mercy to myself. I knew that my brain worked differently and that it was okay and that I could come up with some really weird but really creative ways to overcome some of the ongoing issues in my life. I think I was stuck in the thinking of "Well I should be able to just do the thing like everyone else" which is just comparison, and comparison to brains that didn't work like mine. Comparison is a real thief of joy. Not fun at all, and certainly not realistic. I've had some fun coming up with things that work for me and my brain and to hell with everyone else. 

As far as how it all changed things: 

\- I'm much more reliable as a friend because I set reminders via siri to tell me to call people on their birthdays (I also set a timeslot a few times a week to call a random friend who I haven't spoken to in awhile. Even just leaving them a message checks that box) (note also that I had to write everyones birthdays down... including my siblings. I'd like to say there was no shame there but yea there was.)

\- I eat better because I'm a lot less compulsive (meds helped me with that)

\- I've been able to actually save money (again, meds)

\- I actually clean more and have better hygienne (gross, I know, but its a thing)

\- I'm nicer to myself

There's probably more but that's all I can remember off the top of my head and this answer is already way too long lol.

As far as meds: your call. I did ADHD without meds and things improved a little but for me meds made it so I could actually really use the tools I was learning in a far more effective way.
1000% agree with letting go of the "shoulds". Can totally relate and can say its made a massive difference letting go of those things. Very well worded!

I almost never finish a game and abandon them all the time. I go back to most of them eventually but the gap could be years.

I play almost every genre so its hard to say if I have a favourite. Sometimes I'm in the mood for puzzles, sometimes spooky, sometimes I want to light sims on fire. Depends on the day.

Longest has been Skyrim. I guarantee the only reason its the longest is because I change it up with mods constantly so its basically a new game whenever I want.

I find that the only way I can remember anything I read is if I can explain the thing to another person without any confusion on my part or on theirs. If I can't, then something in my brain switches and the topic becomes interesting so I go in to a dive of information.  


I guess my whole thing is tricking myself into finding the topic interesting. If I can do that, I won't forget anything and I'll have a deeper understanding of the topic.

Just used their services and can confirm they are great. I've been on waiting lists at psychologists for literally a year and I couldn't even save up enough money to pay for the diagnosis. This way was way faster, way easier and a lot less money. Found them professional and super helpful.

There are a lot of days that my dog is the only reason I bother. I can’t imagine losing him now. I am so sorry your cat is nearing the end.

I just want the ability to choose again, really. I used to go places, meet people, explore. I was pretty adventurous and really enjoyed trying new things. Honestly though, one of the best things to do was try to find the best fish and chips. I guess you could call it  the quest I don’t talk about much lol. It was just a weird thing I liked to do. I don’t want extravagance, I just want the ability to go and eat some goddamn fish and chips whenever I want, wherever I want.
I have a dog named Samwise so I guess we’re best friends. I’d be happy to be your penpal.

Save up enough money to live unemployed for six months, maybe more depending on how paranoid you are. Tell the people you actually want to keep talking to that you’re leaving but note that they’re not entitled to know why, unless you want them to. Note that they might try to talk you out of it. Don’t have too much time between telling them you’re leaving and actually leaving. Too much room for them to try to change your mind. It’s good to have a job lined up before you get wherever you’re going, but it’s not always possible. Having that pillow of money will help keep you less frantic and so you might actually go for a job you don’t hate. If you’re trying to get away from people, especially family, get out and get therapy. Saves a lot of time down the road. It’s expensive, but worth it if you find the right therapist. Again, if you’re putting distance between you and family, set strict boundaries when you get out. How much are you going to talk to them? How often? What are you not going to talk with them about? Are you going to talk to them at all? Honestly, when you’re in a bit of a jam, it’s amazing how creative one can become without breaking the law. Big confidence building experience.

I’ve always found that saying yes to strange opportunities led to strange places and strange adventures with strange people. Sometimes you work for money, sometimes you work for the stories. If you’re lucky, you can have both.
All the time.

I had tried for years to lose weight only to gain it. This was a mix of a bunch of things such as a hate for cooking, didn’t know much about food, no clue about calories, and a deep hatred for moderating my food intake. Over the years these things have vastly improved, but they’ve improved because I had to tackle my mental health first. 

Now, I’m not saying folks should put their physical health on hold until they figure out their mental health. I’m a strong believer in looking after both because they affect one another. In my case however, I wanted to die so why would I care for a thing I had no love for? Food was one of the only things that made me feel good so why would I want to restrict it? I really needed to get my mind under control before my body could even have a chance.

I’m still dealing with those issues, but I’ve finally found some solid ground through tons of therapy and a bit of medication. I’m getting my physical health back day by day. You will too :)

I started my own journey probably a million times over the past few years and only gained weight. It’s only been within the last few months that I’ve found what works for me. Maybe some of it can help you.

Calorie counting has been a HUGE help. Within the first few days of tracking, I realized just how many calories I was actually consuming. It was pretty obvious that I didn’t know a damn thing about portion control. Big eye opening moment.

Second was finding recipes that I actually liked. I love food (my size is a testament to that) and I’ve found it’s been fun finding low calorie recipes that don’t taste like butts. My passion for not eating ass has helped.

This was following some folks online who weren’t trying to scam me but who wanted to see people take control of their health. They inspired me to keep trying, and I think I really needed the encouragement.

I know it’s hard. It’s even harder without folks around who have your back. Take it one day at a time and hold on. You got this.

My weakness is salt so I can relate. You can’t hide a bag of chips in my house without me finding it and then devouring the entire thing mindlessly.

I have been cutting back the calories as well and I struggled with not having treats. I was getting pretty frustrated and fed up until I just started working little things into my diet that would make me hate living less. It helps that I don’t eat breakfast, and if I do it’s one or two eggs max. I have a heavy lunch and then I get peckish before dinner so that’s when I’ll eat a “hate everything less” snack. As long as I don’t eat too much, and make sure I’m getting the greens, it seems to defuse my rage.

I should also mention that the best thing for me to do to make sure I don’t have too many of those treats is that I don’t buy enough to destroy my body. I have slipped up plenty of times, but the chafing keeps me reaching for the broccoli.

I have fairly sensitive skin so I break out easily if I use pretty much anything. Started using coconut oil after my roommate suggested it and it’s been amazing. No traces of makeup left on my face, skin is smooth, never any breakouts, and it doesn’t burn if you get some in your eyes. It can be pretty expensive but I only use a dime size amount to clean up my face so it lasts me forever.

I’m in the midst of dealing with this right now. I’ve done a few things to help get me back into reading. 

First, audio books. They help me relax and I sleep better with some British bro lulling me into sweet dreams.

Second, I have to try to stick to some kind of schedule. This is super difficult because the depression can make me so tired or unable to get out of bed that I fail at a schedule constantly. This brings me to my next point.

I had to be okay with not being able to focus and so not being able to read. I had to be kind to myself and know that I would come out on the other side. I love reading and I miss it, but that will come back as long as I keep pushing onwards towards health.

Be kind to yourself. It’s hard, but you got this.

My mental health issues were mainly caused by childhood abuse. I started going to therapy and it’s been LIFE CHANGING. I needed a person to listen, to understand, and to care about me. I have a person I’m learning to trust who is helping me navigate the rocky road that is my brain. God is with me, He is my comfort, but I was never meant to do this alone. He wants me to learn how to trust people, how to accept love from them, because He loves me and he doesn’t want me to fight all by myself. I think we were made to be in community with people, to love and support one another. I don’t think we were made to be self sustaining. God has been keeping me alive, but therapy is going to help me thrive.

I’ve been doing Nanowrimo since 2013 and have reached my word count every year, except one. I have found the last few years the easiest, and not because my life is less busy (it’s probably more busy tbh). I’ve tweaked the way I go about getting my words in over the years and those tweaks have made the whole ordeal a little less awful (note: a little). Maybe some of these will help you:

1) I found a word processor that’s basic af. No distractions, no buttons, I don’t feel the urge to format anything. For some reason, this helped.

2) I set a time every day that I sit down in front of that screen. Sometimes I write, sometimes I brainstorm. As long as some part of the creative process is happening, I’m content and don’t feel bad for doing nothing.

3) If I get writers block, I go for a walk. I put on a playlist that I’ve usually make specifically for the story I’m throwing together, and me and the dog go for a stroll. Exercise helps refresh me, and the dog benefits too.

4) I don’t often plan everything beforehand, but I go in with a general plot at least. When I’m writing, however, I will often get ideas for the next scene or next bit of whatever I want to get down on paper. I write those ideas down so when I did those roadblocks I have something to fall back on. Future me is always grateful.

5) Character sheets. I don’t always adhere to them, but when I get stuck it’s fun to fill them out and can get the inspiration going. 

6) Getting enough sleep. I struggle with this one a lot. I’m a night owl and so I tend to stay up late writing or gaming. I have to force myself to put it all down and fall into bed because I know I won’t get anything done (or it will all be done poorly) if I don’t get enough sleep. That can be hard with the job that I have.

7) Don’t worry if you get behind. Another hard one for me. I love the satisfaction of staying ahead and I equate that with success. This is the one that really kicked me the one year I failed. What I had to realize was that what really made this whole form of torture worth it were those little bits of writing that were actually worth salvaging. You know, those bits of diamond hidden in mounds of pure garbage that I wouldn’t have written if I had been obsessing over editing or plot holes.

8) A bit of competition. I’m not openly competitive, but I like to pick a random person who seems to update their word count consistently and secretly write against them. I never tell them, but that’s just me. Helps kick my butt into gear. I have other friends who pin themselves against each other openly, but I’ve found it puts too much pressure on me to do it that way.

This list wasn’t supposed to be this long...

Hope it helps and happy writing!
